A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same modularity theory and share substantial theoretical and experimental content. All 47 pages of v1 and 40 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original autoencoder and RNN experiments, Isaac3D evaluations, neuroscience-task simulations, and a reanalysis of Xie et al.'s neural recordings.

after.justification: v2 retains original feedforward, Isaac3D, frequency-generation, teacher-student, and entorhinal-inspired RNN experiments, despite removing several neuroscience applications.

M1.justification: The central autoencoder/RNN framework, biological constraints, and CInfoM method remain unchanged. An auxiliary analysis procedure disappears: v1 Appendix H.2's pairwise-difference estimator for recovering coding subspaces from sequences sampled without replacement, together with H.3's construction of data-derived cue encodings.

E1.justification: v2 removes the Xie and Panichello–Buschman working-memory applications, single/dual-reach motor tasks, and Warden–Miller sequential-memory modelling. These are distinct tasks and biological settings. Synthetic autoencoding, Isaac3D, periodic and teacher-student RNN tasks, and spatial/reward/object-tracking coverage remain.

E2.justification: The retained support-versus-statistical-interdependence comparisons and constrained-versus-unconstrained network comparisons use the same alternatives. No changed baseline algorithm set is established. The deleted neuroscience variants primarily concern sampling, encoding, task controls, and evaluation metrics.

E3.justification: The removed studies take away distinct evaluation protocols: working-memory subspace correlations and angles, cue-sampling procedures, and motor alignment measured using PCA components explaining more than 0.1% of variance. Retained experiments preserve their documented datasets, metrics, network sizes, and training budgets; no rerun or setting change is established for them.

E4.justification: v2 drops the principal-angle noise-bias simulations in v1 Appendix H.1, memory-encoding sensitivity analyses in I.1–I.2, and the dual-reach control separating preparation from movement in Figure 5. The retained corner-cutting, correlation, missing-source, and biological-constraint analyses are substantially unchanged.

E5.justification: Deletion of v1 Appendix H removes uncertainty estimation through 200 half-neuron subsamples and the reported 1,000 noise realizations for angle-estimator checks. Retained reporting practices remain unchanged, including Figure 2's standard-error bands and the five random seeds documented for what-where experiments.

E6.justification: v2 removes the working-memory alignment results, motor-subspace findings, sequential stimulus-time responses, and associated appendix outcomes, including Figure 21's 89.95-degree mean principal angle. Retained feedforward, recurrent, and entorhinal results match after relocation and renumbering. The revision does not establish improved performance under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: Corollaries 2.3/B.3 lose the range-symmetry assumption and receive a replacement proof. New Appendices C and D derive sufficient modularity conditions for other activity penalties and multidimensional sources, addressing topics left open in v1. The extensions distinguish p>1 from the L1 case, where equally optimal mixed solutions may remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction withdraw the contributions explaining conflicting prefrontal working-memory findings and motor-subspace orthogonality. Neuroscience contributions now center on entorhinal representations and alternative explanations of mixed selectivity. The exact linear-autoencoder claim remains, while Section 2.4 adds claims of theoretical generalization to other norms and multidimensional sources.

C2.justification: The discussion replaces the absence of norm/multidimensional theory with the narrower limitation that necessary conditions remain unresolved. It adds explicit biological omissions and calls for testing beyond entorhinal cortex. Earlier motor and sequential-processing explanations, and detailed prefrontal model-data discrepancies and orthogonality-versus-modularity caveats, disappear with those applications.

D1.justification: v2 removes substantial neural-data processing, cue-encoding, and task-specific model documentation from v1 Appendices H and I.1–I.4. Implementation details for retained experiments largely survive in renumbered appendices. The reproducibility instruction changes its repository destination from dont-cut-corners to modular; the PDFs alone do not establish repository availability or contents.

R1.justification: Research positioning narrows through removal of the working-memory, motor, and sequential-processing literature connections. Appendix A adds a dedicated grid-cell-modules discussion, citing Burak and Fiete, Mathis et al., and Wei et al. to distinguish existing circuit/coding accounts from normative explanations of module emergence. Core positioning relative to independence-based disentanglement and matrix factorization remains.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, and the abstract, introduction, intuition, and discussion are revised. The main narrative is reorganized around entorhinal applications, with missing-source analysis incorporated there. New Sections 2.4–2.5 and theoretical appendices restructure the exposition, while former neuroscience sections and appendices are removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn, enlarged, and relocated, with expanded visual explanation of encoding costs. v1 Figures 4–5 and 19–23 disappear. Figure 7 is reduced to its missing-source panels and becomes Figure 5; other retained figures are resized, relocated, or relabelled, including Figure 6 becoming Figure 4.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the central exposition and addresses explicit theoretical limitations through the revised corollary and new sufficient-condition arguments. However, it also removes original neural-data reanalysis and several biological validation studies with their controls. Narrower claims partly accommodate this loss, but the tradeoff between broader theory and reduced empirical grounding does not establish a clear net quality improvement or deterioration.
